title: Ecosystems in a Flask
endLine: Hold conditions fixed in replicated microcosms to test one ecological cause.

scenes.tts: How do you test one ecological rule when wild nature never holds still? In a forest or pond, food, weather, predators and competitors all shift together. To untangle them, ecologists build small, simple communities in vessels on a laboratory bench.
scenes.caption: How do you test one ecological rule when wild nature never holds still? In a forest or pond, food, weather, predators and competitors all shift together. To untangle them, ecologists build small, simple communities in vessels on a laboratory bench.
scenes.visual: Schematic outdoor pond and forest edge with swirling food, weather, predator and competitor arrows shifting at once; the scene contracts smoothly into a neat row of small clear glass culture vessels on a dark laboratory bench, tiny glowing microbes drifting inside.
scenes.narration: How do you test one ecological rule when wild nature never holds still? In a forest or pond, food, weather, predators and competitors all shift together. To untangle them, ecologists build small, simple communities in vessels on a laboratory bench.

scenes.visual: Keep the lit glass vessels alive on the dark bench with slowly drifting microbes; fade in the title 'Ecosystems in a Flask' above them for two seconds, then fade it out.

scenes.tts: These are laboratory microcosms, small replicated cultures. They hold yeasts, bacteria, ciliates, algae or rotifers, fast enough to follow many generations in weeks. Some run in tubes, a fraction moved into fresh medium each day. Others run in a chemostat, a vessel with a steady nutrient inflow and matching outflow.

scenes.tts: In a microcosm, you hold conditions fixed and replicate communities to test one ecological cause. Take soil bacteria in tubes refreshed every twenty-four hours. The share discarded each day acts like a death rate on everyone. At low dilution, one slow grower excluded a faster-growing competitor.
scenes.caption: In a microcosm, you hold conditions fixed and replicate communities to test one ecological cause. Take soil bacteria in tubes refreshed every 24 hours. The share discarded each day acts like a death rate on everyone. At low dilution, one slow grower excluded a faster-growing competitor.
scenes.visual: Replicate mixed tubes sit on the bench beside a dilution dial set low and a 24-hour clock hand sweeping; green slow-growing bacteria multiply and crowd out amber faster-growing bacteria while a pipette removes a small share each cycle; a schematic trace below shows green rising and amber falling to zero.
scenes.narration: In a microcosm, you hold conditions fixed and replicate communities to test one ecological cause. Take soil bacteria in tubes refreshed every 24 hours. The share discarded each day acts like a death rate on everyone. At low dilution, one slow grower excluded a faster-growing competitor.

scenes.tts: Now turn the dilution dial up, discarding a much larger share each day. Both species lose the same fraction of cells. Predict: does the slow grower still win, or does the faster grower take over?
scenes.caption: Now turn the dilution dial up, discarding a much larger share each day. Both species lose the same fraction of cells. Predict: does the slow grower still win, or does the faster grower take over?
scenes.visual: The dilution dial rotates from low to high; a larger volume drains out of each tube and fresh clear medium pours in, flushing both green and amber cells equally; the schematic population trace pauses at a glowing question mark with two diverging dotted paths.
scenes.narration: Now turn the dilution dial up, discarding a much larger share each day. Both species lose the same fraction of cells. Predict: does the slow grower still win, or does the faster grower take over?

scenes.visual: Hold the question 'Slow grower or faster grower?' on screen while the high-dilution tubes gently pulse and the two dotted schematic trajectories shimmer.

scenes.tts: In 2019, Abreu and colleagues saw the winner flip: the faster grower won. In the model, each species' carrying capacity, the most its tube can hold, shrinks by death rate over growth rate. A slow grower has the smaller growth rate, so it loses the bigger share. Monocultures, each species grown alone, check that a lost species could have survived that dilution.

scenes.visual: In the high-dilution mixed tubes, amber cells surge while green cells vanish and the schematic trace follows the upper amber path. The words 'carrying capacity shrinks by death rate ÷ growth rate' write on screen as spoken; the same death rate divides into a small green growth bar and a large amber growth bar, so the green capacity bar loses the larger share (schematic, no numbers). Beside the mixed tubes, a green monoculture tube lights up with surviving cells, showing green persists alone.

scenes.tts: In 2012, Hall and colleagues crossed disturbance frequency with intensity in bacterial microcosms. Different combinations gave different diversity curves, so single-factor tests miss interactions. In 2016, Gibbons and colleagues found that replacing culture with fresh medium also resupplied nutrients. So killing cells and feeding them were not fully separated. Vessels stay simple: they test mechanisms, not wild outcomes.

One tube shows a double arrow for cells removed and fresh nutrients entering together. A crisp glass boundary ring frames the bench against a faint distant wild landscape.

scenes.tts: These tiny worlds unlocked landmark findings. In 1934, Georgii Gause reported Paramecium species grown alone and together. Alone, each grew well. Together, Paramecium aurelia persisted while Paramecium caudatum declined toward disappearance. That pattern was later named competitive exclusion: complete competitors cannot coexist.

scenes.visual: Tubes labelled 'Gause 1934' show two ciliate species each rising and levelling off alone; then in a mixed tube one persists while the other fades on a schematic curve. The phrase 'competitive exclusion' appears under the mixed tube.

scenes.tts: In 1958, C B Huffaker kept predatory and prey mites on oranges with partial barriers. Numbers rose and fell three times before the run ended. It made a case that spatial structure can prolong a predator-prey interaction.
scenes.caption: In 1958, C. B. Huffaker kept predatory and prey mites on oranges with partial barriers. Numbers rose and fell three times before the run ended. It made a case that spatial structure can prolong a predator-prey interaction.
scenes.visual: Beside the tubes on the same bench, a schematic array of oranges with partial barriers labelled 'Huffaker 1958' pulses through three successive predator-prey wave peaks, then the trace stops at a marked 'run ended' line.
scenes.narration: In 1958, C. B. Huffaker kept predatory and prey mites on oranges with partial barriers. Numbers rose and fell three times before the run ended. It made a case that spatial structure can prolong a predator-prey interaction.

scenes.tts: In 2003, Yoshida and colleagues grew rotifers grazing algae in chemostats. One algal clone cannot evolve by selection; a mix of clones can. With one clone, rotifer peaks followed algae by about a quarter cycle.
scenes.caption: In 2003, Yoshida and colleagues grew rotifers grazing algae in chemostats. One algal clone cannot evolve by selection; a mix of clones can. With one clone, rotifer peaks followed algae by about a quarter cycle.
scenes.visual: Back on the bench, a chemostat pair labelled 'Yoshida et al. 2003': one vessel holds identical algae of one colour ('one clone'), the other a mix of colours ('many clones'), rotifers grazing in both. The single-clone vessel drives a schematic wave where rotifer peaks trail algal peaks by a quarter cycle.
scenes.narration: In 2003, Yoshida and colleagues grew rotifers grazing algae in chemostats. One algal clone cannot evolve by selection; a mix of clones can. With one clone, rotifer peaks followed algae by about a quarter cycle.

scenes.tts: With many clones, cycles ran long and peaks moved largely out of step. Algae that resisted grazing were poorer competitors for nutrients. That made the case for prey evolution driving the cycles.
scenes.caption: With many clones, cycles ran long and peaks moved largely out of step. Algae that resisted grazing were poorer competitors for nutrients. That made the case for prey evolution driving the cycles.
scenes.visual: The multiclonal vessel stretches into a long schematic wave with rotifer and algal peaks largely out of step. As the trade-off is spoken, a defended alga gets a shield icon and a smaller nutrient-uptake arrow than an undefended one (schematic).
scenes.narration: With many clones, cycles ran long and peaks moved largely out of step. Algae that resisted grazing were poorer competitors for nutrients. That made the case for prey evolution driving the cycles.
